title: Collective advantage from a minimal record in a quantum information engine
authors: Kangqiao Liu, Jie Gu, Deyou Chen
abstract: For a single particle, a quantum information engine can turn measurement fluctuations into transport by raising a barrier behind the particle each time its position is measured. When many particles are present, the barrier still depends on just one number, the position of the leftmost particle, so we let the demon measure that order statistic and nothing else. A demon that resolves every position instead pays a record entropy that grows with particle number, even though the extra distinctions never change where the barrier is placed. We show that the coarser measurement supplies an energy that is bounded independently of particle number, and that this bound yields a ceiling on the record entropy that falls as the filling increases. At the same tilt, the collective engine then delivers $44\%$ more work per recorded nat than independent single-particle engines, each with its own optimized cycle time and each running at equal or greater power per particle. Pauli blocking ends this advantage once the accessible region just above the wall fills. We also evaluate the coherence that the coarse measurement leaves behind, and the cost of placing the barrier imprecisely.
summary: This work analyzes a quantum information engine using fermions on a lattice, comparing two measurement protocols: measuring the full particle configuration versus measuring only the leftmost particle's position. The authors demonstrate that the coarse measurement strategy yields a substantial, particle-number-independent advantage in work extraction efficiency over measuring the full state, providing insights into fundamental limits of quantum work extraction.
main_problem: The paper compares the work extraction and record entropy generated by two measurement strategies in a quantum information engine: measuring the full particle configuration versus measuring only the order statistic (leftmost particle position).
main_result: The coarse measurement (order statistic) supplies energy bounded independently of particle number and delivers significantly more work per recorded nat than independent single-particle engines.
method: The analysis uses a four-step quantum engine cycle involving measurement (Lüders type), feedback (wall placement), unitary evolution, and recording, comparing the entropy cost of different measurement resolutions.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as N spin-polarized fermions on a one-dimensional tilted lattice of M sites, governed by a Hamiltonian involving hopping and a tilt potential. The engine operates by using measurement outcomes to advance a hard wall barrier.
key_observables: Work extracted per cycle, record entropy rate (H), and the ratio of work/entropy compared to single-particle engines.
important_parameters: The tilt parameter $\alpha = \Delta/J$, the particle number $N$, and the lattice size $M$.
main_assumptions: The measurement is assumed to be of the Lüders type, and the analysis compares the two demons while both follow the same four-step cycle.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the difference between full-configuration and order-statistic measurement outcomes, showing the record entropy rate for both strategies. Figure 2 compares the stored work and corresponding record entropy rate for the order-statistic demon.
paper_structure: The paper develops the framework by defining the engine cycle and comparing the information cost of full vs. coarse measurements. It derives energy bounds and shows that the coarse measurement maintains a significant work advantage over independent engines, limited by Pauli blocking.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, quantitative comparison of information processing limits in a many-body quantum system, directly linking measurement back-action (information cost) to thermodynamic work extraction in a lattice model.

FIG. 4. Pauli blocking suppresses wall motion as the acces- sible region fills. The no-advance probability qN is shown against particle number for three representative tilts. The dotted line marks complete blocking, qN = 1. The short mark on the horizontal axis indicates the Bloch-excursion scale 4J/∆for α = 0.5.

Figure 4 makes the approach to blocking explicit. As the particle number grows, qN approaches one and the minimum rarely leaves the origin. The exact inequality in Eq. (19) already forces this trend at large N. Once the advances become very rare, assigning a unique inte- ger stall point depends on how long they are observed. We therefore use the continuous growth of qN as the mi- croscopic signature of blocking. The useful collective regime lies at intermediate filling, before Pauli exclu- sion suppresses both wall motion and record production.
